definition: Capricious means subject to whim; changing unpredictably.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word capricious. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know capricious should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Three-year-olds are capricious diners — yesterday's beloved noodles are today's outrage, and no menu survives the week.
Changeable weather shifts often, but often for reasons a forecaster can map; capricious cuts deeper — change with no pattern or cause at all.
A temperamental engine acts up when it's cold, and you learn its moods; capricious goes further, swinging on pure whim that no one can learn.

Flighty describes a person who is scattered and easily distracted — attention fluttering off mid-sentence — and it stays light, almost fond. Capricious is heavier: the changes follow no reason at all, and someone is usually stuck paying for the whim — a capricious ruler, a capricious referee.

Arbitrary means decided without any reason — the cutoff was forty because someone said forty. What it does not require is motion: an arbitrary choice can be made once and never revisited, while capricious decisions keep changing, whim after whim, each reversing the last.

Fickle is about likings and loyalties that switch fast — a fickle fan drops the team after one lost game. Capricious is wider and harder to live under: not just affections but rulings and demands shifting on pure whim, with no pattern anyone can learn.

Capricious arrived in English as one sealed piece, and its Italian parts built nothing else here — so there is no everyday English cousin to find. Its closest kin is its own noun, caprice: a stray whim.
Capricious means subject to whim; changing unpredictably.
The house cat has decided, this Tuesday, that the blue armchair is the only acceptable throne; by Thursday the armchair no longer merits a glance and only the laundry basket will do.
Offer a reason and you'll be wrong by the weekend.
Her affections are capricious — governed by whim, and by nothing else anyone can name.
Capricious is stronger than changeable: plenty of things change on schedule or for reasons — tides, moods before coffee.
A capricious mind changes without pattern or cause, so no one can prepare for it; that whiff of power over everyone waiting on the whim is the word's signature.
Capricious passes judgment: it says the changes have no reason and everyone else pays for the whim — capricious rulings, capricious weather.
Its neighbor in this unit, dynamic, treats ceaseless change as life and energy; call a market dynamic and you praise it, call it capricious and you warn people off.

Court painters under Duke Ercole learned to keep their bags half packed.
His patronage was capricious: a portraitist showered with gold in March might be barred from the palace by May, then summoned back in June as though nothing had happened.
Chroniclers hunted for a method in it — some test of loyalty, some hidden ledger of favors — and found none.
The duke gained nothing by the reversals; taxes, wars, and advisors all stayed the same while the favor wheeled about.
Painters who thrived learned the only rule available: expect nothing, and keep a second patron in another city.
